body.html: Public health uses several complementary approaches, linked to underlying health models (biomedical, behavioural, socio-environmental): disease prevention, health promotion, primary health care and the One Health approach. This lecture contrasts the two main ones.

Measures that aim not only to prevent the onset of disease (fighting risk factors) but also to stop its progress and reduce its consequences (WHO glossary, 1984). It requires an identified disease process, diagnostic and intervention means, and known economic, social and ethical aspects. Mapped on the natural history of disease: primary prevention reduces incidence (new cases) before exposure: immunisation, health education, smoking cessation; based on relative risk in exposed vs non-exposed people; the most cost-effective. Secondary prevention: early detection and intervention, ideally before clinical signs: cancer screening, tuberculin skin tests, contact investigations; screening is justified when the disease is frequent enough to cause excess (premature) mortality and cost, an effective treatment exists, and mass early diagnosis is feasible. Tertiary prevention: reduce the prevalence of chronic disability and recurrence: physiotherapy, rehabilitation, social and professional reintegration, palliative care, surveillance of former cancer patients. Prevention has been essential and is a major tool, but it is a directive model, less adapted to chronic non-communicable diseases and social determinants.

Launched by WHO at the Ottawa conference (1986): the process of enabling people to increase control over their health and its determinants. Health is a capital resource, and all sectors must participate. Prerequisites for health: peace, shelter, education, food, income, a stable ecosystem, sustainable resources, social justice and equity. Characteristics: holistic, participatory, focused on determinants (social, behavioural, economic, environmental), on strengths not only deficits, with multiple complementary strategies.

Five action pillars: (1) build healthy public policy (policies shaping living conditions; actors: politicians, influencers/lobbies, the public, the media; tools: advocacy, health impact assessment, intersectoral action, since social inequalities in health arise mainly outside the care system); (2) create supportive environments (physical, psychological, organisational: education, transport, housing, urban planning, workplaces; e.g. health-promoting schools); (3) strengthen community action (mobilisation, participation, empowerment; community = shared belonging; e.g. community dialogue); (4) develop personal skills (health literacy: finding, understanding and using health information, e.g. linking smoking to cancer); (5) reorient health services (rebalance responsibility between professionals and citizens; 'co-produced' services giving patients a voice, access to records, a say in organisation).

Disease prevention: biomedical and epidemiological model; vertical approach by programmes; the population as object; focus on risk factors; individual responsibility. Health promotion: bio-psycho-social model; horizontal approach through living environments; the population as subject, in collaboration; multifactorial, focused on strengths and advantages; determinants of health. Health promotion and social determinants are the major issues for public health's future, aiming at quality of life, not just life expectancy.

Biostatistics allows the description, comparison and interpretation of health phenomena using data. The study guide distinguishes biostatistic (the science of studying biological and medical data) from biostatistics (the indicators, measures and tests derived from it). The right analysis depends on the nature of the data, the variables and the question asked.

A variable is a characteristic that can be measured or collected; a value is a possible answer for a quantitative variable, a category (modality) for a qualitative one. Qualitative: nominal (no order: sex, blood group) or ordinal (ordered: pain mild/moderate/severe, disease stage). Quantitative: discrete (integers: number of children) or continuous (any value: height, weight, blood pressure). The dependent variable is the outcome you want to explain or predict. Study designs: cross-sectional (one point in time, a snapshot), cohort (follows people from exposure to outcome), case-control (compares people with and without the disease).

Frequencies, percentages, mean (sum / number), median (middle value when sorted), mode (most frequent value), standard deviation, minimum and maximum; range = maximum − minimum. In a normal (Gaussian) distribution the curve is symmetric and bell-shaped and mean = median = mode; a non-normal distribution is skewed. Normality is checked with the Shapiro-Wilk test: H₀ = data are normal; W closer to 1 = more normal; with α = 0.05, p > 0.05 → normality not rejected (treated as normal), p ≤ 0.05 → not normal (e.g. W = 0.97, p = 0.12 normal; W = 0.85, p = 0.001 not normal).

Graphs: nominal → bar chart (or pie); ordinal → ordered bar chart; discrete → bar chart; continuous → histogram (shape) or box plot (median, IQR, outliers; compares groups).

Two qualitative variables: chi-square test (Fisher's exact test for small samples). One qualitative + one quantitative: Student's t-test if normal, Mann-Whitney if not. Two quantitative: Pearson correlation if normal, Spearman if not. Always identify variable types, study design and distribution first. Data cleaning (check missing values, duplicates, inconsistencies, coding errors) ensures valid, reproducible, unbiased results. Statistical inference uses a sample to draw conclusions about a population, through hypothesis testing with a null hypothesis and a significance level (usually 5%).

Determinants of health are the factors that influence the health of individuals and communities. They can be sorted by three questions about people: who they are, what they do and in which conditions they live. They are modifiable or non-modifiable, act as risk or protective factors, and operate at individual, social and environmental levels. The modifiable ones guide public health interventions to prevent disease and promote health.

title: Modifiable and non-modifiable: the CVD example
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.html: Non-modifiable: age (over 83% of people who die of heart disease are 65 or older), sex (men at greater and earlier risk), family history (father with a heart attack before 55 or mother before 65), ethnic origin (e.g. African or South Asian). Modifiable: smoking (plaque build-up, less oxygen, higher blood pressure), physical inactivity (aim for at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-to-vigorous activity), poor nutrition (saturated fat, few fruits and vegetables), overweight/obesity (about 1 in 10 premature deaths in Canadian adults 20-64), high blood pressure (above 140/90 mmHg, or 130/80 in diabetes), high LDL cholesterol, uncontrolled diabetes, excessive alcohol (limit to 10 drinks a week for women, 15 for men, per the lecture's source) and stress.

Protective factors are attributes (skills, strengths, resources) that shield people from developing or worsening health problems and help them cope. Risk factors contribute to developing or worsening problems: e.g. oppositional behaviour, family conflict and social isolation raise the risk of mood disorders and substance use. Examples: older people and those with underlying conditions were at higher risk of severe COVID-19; smoking's many consequences (US Surgeon General's report, 2014); climate and environment.

title: Weighting the determinants and social determinants
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.html: Models such as Dever (1976) estimated the contribution of each type of determinant (lifestyle, environment, biology, health system). One consequence was to make individuals responsible for their behaviour (tobacco, diet, obesity, vaccination), which raises a fairness question since behaviours depend on conditions. Social determinants of health (Marmot, The Health Gap, 2015; WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health, Solar and Irwin framework, 2007): education and childhood (more education, longer healthier life; poverty, disability and discrimination in childhood lead to heart disease, diabetes, depression; poverty stress affects brain development), neighbourhood and built environment (housing, transport, healthy food, air and water, crime), and social and community support. A health problem like smoking or junk food can be traced as a chain from individual to strategic, policy level. Conclusion: a new way to see public health, with health promotion approaches.

Epidemiology (epi = upon, demos = people, -logy = science: 'what falls upon people') is the basic science of preventive and social medicine. The standard definition (J. Last, 1988): the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to the prevention and control of health problems. Distribution: time, person, place; determinants: biological, chemical, physical, social, cultural, economic, genetic and behavioural factors; health-related states: diseases, causes of death, behaviours, positive health, service use; specified populations: groups rather than individuals; application: promote, protect and restore health. Its ultimate aims: eliminate or reduce health problems and promote the well-being of society.

Hippocrates (400 BCE, On Airs, Waters and Places): rational, environmental and behavioural explanations of disease. Ibn al-Khatib (14th century, treatise on the plague) described transmission by contagion centuries before Pasteur, during the Black Death in al-Andalus. John Graunt (1662): first quantification of births, deaths and disease patterns (sex differences, infant mortality, urban/rural, seasons) from London bills of mortality. James Lind (1747): one of the first controlled clinical trials: 12 scurvy sailors in 6 groups; those given lemons and limes recovered. William Farr (1800s): father of modern vital statistics, surveillance and disease classification. John Snow (1813-1858): London Soho cholera outbreaks (1849-54), leading to reform of water and waste systems. From 1950, non-infectious 'diseases of civilisation' (Doll and Hill smoking study); since 1970, all health phenomena and new fields (intervention, pharmaco-, genetic epidemiology).

Endemic: constant presence of a disease in a population. Epidemic: occurrence in excess of the usual expected level in a population or area. Pandemic: epidemic widespread across a country or the world. Approach: (1) ask questions (what, how much, who, where, when, why), (2) make comparisons (diseased vs non-diseased, exposed vs unexposed). Components: frequency (rates: incidence, prevalence; ratios: sex ratio, doctor-population ratio), distribution (descriptive: generates hypotheses) and determinants (analytic: tests hypotheses).

Observational: descriptive (who, what, where, when; e.g. tracking measles by age, vaccination status and location to target campaigns) and analytical (the 'how': case-control and cohort studies identifying risk factors; e.g. a cohort exposed vs unexposed to industrial air pollution showing more respiratory disease, leading to regulation). Experimental/interventional: randomised controlled trials (e.g. a new diabetes drug vs placebo), field trials, community trials. Evidence pyramid (top to bottom): systematic reviews, RCTs, cohort studies, case-control studies, case series, case reports, ideas/editorials/opinions, in vitro research.

A health indicator is a quantitative measure reflecting a health condition, trend or factor in a population, used to describe how healthy it is, show changes over time, and assess programmes and policies (e.g. incidence, proportion of children immunised). Domains (WHO 100 core indicators): health status (life expectancy, malaria mortality), risk factors (stunting under 5, safe sanitation), service coverage (antenatal coverage, TB case detection), health systems (hospital bed density, health expenditure as % of GDP). They let us monitor health, plan and allocate resources, evaluate programmes and compare across time and place.

Metrics: counts, calculations (percentages, rates, ratios), indices and composite measures (e.g. DALY: disability-adjusted life years) and thresholds. Exposure (risk factor, independent variable: smoking) vs disease (outcome, dependent variable: lung cancer). The population at risk must be estimated correctly (e.g. only women for cervical cancer). Proportion: unitless fraction with a characteristic (prevalence). Rate: speed of occurrence over time (incidence). Ratio: one quantity divided by another (male:female 12:11). Example rate: 9 diabetes cases in 3,000 people over 2 years = 9 / (3,000 × 2) = 1.5 per 1,000 person-years.

The frequency of existing cases in a population at a given time: useful to assess needs for prevention, care and service planning, especially for conditions with gradual onset. Point prevalence: at one moment (80 of 1,000 mothers say their child has diarrhoea today = 8%). Period prevalence: over a period, e.g. annual or lifetime prevalence ('Have you ever had asthma?' 100/1,000 = 10%). Unspecified prevalence usually means point prevalence. Example: 400 of 5,000 dorm students had flu during winter term = 8%.

The number of new cases in a specified period in a population at risk (those already ill are excluded from the denominator). Cumulative incidence (risk, incidence proportion): new cases / population at risk at the start; needs follow-up of a closed cohort; e.g. 50 breast cancers among 10,000 women over 40 in a year = 5 per 1,000. Incidence rate (incidence density): new cases / sum of disease-free person-time; e.g. 274 strokes in 908,447 person-years = 30.2 per 100,000 person-years (cumulative incidence in the same cohort of 118,539 women = 2.3 per 1,000). When disease is rare (under 5%), incidence rate ≈ incidence proportion. Relationship: in a stable situation, prevalence ≈ incidence × duration; longer disease duration means higher prevalence.

Crude mortality rate: all-cause deaths / mid-period population (USA 2003: 2,419,921 / 290,809,777 × 100,000 = 832.1 per 100,000). Cause-specific mortality rate: deaths from one cause / population (accidents, USA 2003: 37.2 per 100,000). Case fatality: proportion of cases of a disease who die within a specified time, a measure of severity, usually a percentage. Indicators guide evidence-based decisions, policy and resource allocation, and track progress toward health goals.

Health is more than treating a wound. The lecture's case: a 17-year-old arrives at 3 a.m. with a hand cut, but is anxious, avoids eye contact and has left home after a family conflict. Good care is holistic: clinical management (clean, suture, tetanus, antibiotics), psychological support (assess anxiety or depression, refer if needed), social intervention (living conditions, social services) and a multidisciplinary team ensuring continuity and reintegration.

Health (WHO Constitution, 1948): a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. Public health (Winslow): the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health through the organised efforts and informed choices of society, organisations, public and private communities, and individuals.

Clinical approach: targets sick people, when they consult; care at the moment of contact; does not take costs into account; the doctor has the power. Public health approach: targets the whole population, even those who do not consult; acts throughout life and in daily life; takes costs into account; interventions need population participation. WHO: public health covers all organised measures to prevent disease, promote health and prolong life among the population as a whole, focusing on the total system rather than individual patients or one disease.

Three pillars, illustrated with cardiovascular disease (leading cause of death, over 17 million deaths a year, about 31%): prevention (blood pressure screening acts before disease develops, targeting diet, inactivity, smoking, alcohol), health promotion (a 'Move More, Eat Better' city campaign empowers people and creates supportive environments) and organised efforts (COVID-19: ICU capacity, lockdowns, masks, vaccination, adapted schools and media, community support).

Hippocrates, Airs, Waters and Places (5th-4th century BCE): environment and health. Sanitation by Greeks and Romans; Arab medicine in the Middle Ages; the Public Health Act of 1848 in the United Kingdom. 19th century: modern public health in England's industrial cities in response to cholera and typhus. Environmental approach (1840-1870): Chadwick report (1842) on workers' living conditions; John Snow on cholera transmission; Virchow on economic and social factors of typhus. Bacteriological approach (1880-1930): germ theory, Pasteur (rabies vaccine 1885) and Koch (tuberculosis, cholera); state hospitals and dispensaries. Therapeutic era (1930-): insulin, sulphonamides, decline of infections, resources concentrated in curative hospital care, then genetics.

A public health problem is judged by criteria including inequalities and vulnerability (disproportionately affecting the poor, women, children, migrants, the elderly: e.g. tuberculosis) and social perception (seen as alarming, requiring a collective response: e.g. HIV/AIDS in the 1980s-90s). Current issues: non-communicable diseases (about 70% of global deaths; unhealthy diet, inactivity, tobacco, alcohol), infectious diseases (COVID-19, emerging vector-borne diseases with climate change, antimicrobial resistance), health inequalities (poverty, education, access), climate change (extreme weather, pollution, water scarcity) and the mental health crisis (depression, anxiety, substance use, stigma).
